title: OpenAI’s Astra solves 10 long-open math problems and publishes the proofs
teaser: OpenAI's Astra solved ten long-open math problems—including proving a non-sofic group exists since 1999—and published machine-checkable proofs.
summary: OpenAI Group PBC announced that its internal model, Astra, successfully solved ten major open problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science. The company bolstered these claims by publishing machine-checkable proofs via Lean 4 certificates, confirming the lack of unproven steps. Key breakthroughs include constructing a non-sofic group—a question open since 1999—and disproving Connes's rigidity conjecture. Astra also proved Ehrhart's volume conjecture and resolved multiple problems from Paul Erdős’s catalog, such as problem 183 concerning Ramsey numbers. While these results are significant steps for scientific reasoning, the model has not undergone peer review.
author: Duncan Riley
content: OpenAI Group PBC revealed Saturday that an internal version of Astra, the model family it calls its next major release, produced new results for 10 problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science that had been open for at least a decade, and it published machine-checkable proofs alongside the claim. The company posted a 249-page manuscript collection , model-written reasoning walkthroughs and Lean 4 certificates for all 10 results. The certificates sit on GitHub under an Apache 2.0 license, and the repository reports a "sorry" count of zero, meaning no step in any of the formalized proofs has been left unproven. The headline result is an explicit construction of a non-sofic group, a question left open since Mikhail Gromov introduced soficity in 1999. Astra also disproved Connes's rigidity conjecture, constructing infinitely many non-isomorphic groups with property (T) that share the same von Neumann algebra, and it proved Ehrhart's volume conjecture. Three problems from Paul Erdős's catalog fell as well, including problem 183 on multicolor Ramsey numbers. Stripped of the terminology, a group is the mathematical description of a set of symmetries, and a sofic group is one whose structure can be approximated by shuffling a finite deck of cards. Every group anyone had examined turned out to be sofic, and no one could prove that all of them are. Astra built the exception. Connes's conjecture, posed in 1980, held that for one rigid class of groups, a related algebraic object acts as a unique fingerprint, pinning down the group it came from. Astra produced infinitely many distinct groups sharing a single fingerprint. Erdős problem 183 is about Ramsey numbers. Color the links in a network with a fixed number of colors and past a certain size you cannot avoid a triangle whose three links match. The Ramsey number is the size at which that becomes true. The remainder of the list runs across high-dimensional sphere packing, binary and spherical codes, arithmetic circuit complexity, quantum parallel repetition and the hardness of the closest vector problem, the last of which bears on lattice cryptography. Astra also produced counterexamples in extremal graph theory, resolving two more Erdős problems. The Lean certificates are what give the announcement its weight. Lean's kernel returns a binary verdict, either the proof compiles or it does not, which takes trust in the model out of the equation. What it does not take out is the need for a mathematician to confirm that each formal statement says what the open problem actually asks and to judge whether the result matters. None of the 10 has been through peer review. OpenAI has been here before. The company's then vice president of science, Kevin Weil, claimed in October 2025 that GPT-5 had solved 10 previously unsolved Erdős problems. Thomas Bloom, who maintains the erdosproblems.com database, called that "a dramatic misrepresentation." The model had found papers in the literature that Bloom was personally unaware of. Weil deleted the post, and Google DeepMind Chief Executive Demis Hassabis called the episode embarrassing. Bloom called the Astra results "big news" and rated them ahead of the Erdős unit distance counterexample an internal OpenAI model produced in May, a paper he helped verify. Astra itself remains unreleased. OpenAI describes it as a model family built to run long tasks by coordinating multiple agents over extended periods, an extension of the test-time reasoning work associated with research scientist Noam Brown, who called the results "a major step for scientific reasoning" in a post on X. Human researchers turned the model's output into publishable papers, though OpenAI said the mathematical arguments themselves came from Astra. The compute bill was modest. OpenAI put the token cost for all 10 solutions at roughly $2,000 at GPT-5.6 Sol application programming interface rates. Chief Executive Sam Altman demonstrated Astra to policymakers in Washington in recent days. The company has not given a release date, pricing or a decision on whether the model ships as GPT-6 or as another GPT-5 variant, and any launch will run through the federal AI safety review process that already staggered the GPT-5.6 rollout . The timing is awkward for a mathematics community that has been pushing back. In June, the International Mathematical Union endorsed the Leiden Declaration , which warns that AI companies are "using published research without consent, bypassing peer review, and threatening the integrity of proof and attribution." Fernando Borretti, a software engineer who writes on technology, argued in a blog post responding to the release that the usual defenses of human mathematicians no longer hold and that the frontier of the field will recede past the point where anyone can follow it. "We will live in a demon-haunted world, full of marvelous devices whose operation we will not understand," he wrote. title: Meet the 'internet radical' who helped Microsoft get email and AT&T get online
teaser: A 'radical' who pushed tech giants to embrace the web: Tom Evslin helped drive Microsoft’s Exchange and AT&T’s WorldNet, proving the power of decentralized internet communication.
summary:
Tom Evslin, described as an "internet radical," played a crucial role in shaping early tech standards for both Microsoft and AT&T. Working at Microsoft, he advocated that products like Exchange Server should only launch once integrated with the nascent internet, disagreeing with Bill Gates' initial push to delay progress. While corporate policy questioned the security of internet communication, Evslin successfully demonstrated the rising demand for the SMTP gateway, proving the web's power.
Later, AT&T invited him to spearhead their WorldNet strategy. Evslin pushed the company to abandon its historical role as a content provider and instead become an Internet Service Provider (ISP), advocating for rapid deployment and all-you-can-eat pricing models. These efforts culminated in him founding ITXC in 1997 as a wholesale VoIP carrier.
content: OFFBEAT Meet the 'internet radical' who helped Microsoft get email and AT&T get online Tom Evslin on Bill Gates, the birth of Exchange, and dragging Ma Bell onto the web Tom Evslin drove the WorldNet project at AT&T and helped develop what became Microsoft Exchange and Outlook. He was at Microsoft when the company was still working out what to do about this newfangled internet thing. Evslin describes himself as one of Microsoft's "internet radicals" in the early 1990s, when the company was developing Exchange Server to fend off the threat from Lotus Notes. "Bill Gates was willing to put lots of effort and money into Exchange because he was very afraid of Lotus Notes," Evslin says. "He felt that Lotus Notes could become a platform the way that Windows was, which would be an enormous threat to Microsoft. And so he saw Exchange as a Notes killer." Evslin saw Exchange differently "because I was an email guy." He and Microsoft's other "internet radicals" wanted the upcoming products delayed until they had been made relevant to the internet. Gates disagreed. "Bill said, with some truth, that we were probably behind schedule anyway, always looking for an excuse to be late. So we go ahead with the next launch of products, including Office, Exchange, and NT, then worry about the internet afterward, which I thought was a mistake." Evslin was fascinated by the internet's potential and disappointed by Gates' stance. He was responsible for gateways in Exchange, services that connect one mail system to another. Some did things like connecting to CompuServe. Others linked to MCI Mail, one of the first commercial email services in the US, "which I had done a client for," Evslin says. "We had one little gateway that we hadn't put much work into, which was called an SMTP gateway, which connected SMTP mail, which was used on the internet. Which itself wasn't widely used." So, was Gates right? Only briefly. While Microsoft's corporate clients insisted communication over the internet was "not safe" and "not secure," Evslin says: "All of a sudden we got a huge number of requests for this SMTP gateway. And when I looked into it, I found that more and more email was going over the internet." The official corporate stance might have been one of "nope," but employees had other ideas. "Their engineers were communicating on the internet, and they never understood that, or didn't understand that at the time," Evslin says. And then there was what would become Outlook. "From the beginning, we wanted the client for Exchange to be able to support graphics, to be able to support fonts, so that you could format an email in the same way that you could format a Word document. "Where we didn't go far enough is we still had two separate formatting engines, so the Word and Outlook client never merged as I thought they should have." Soon after Gates chose to launch the products before adding deeper internet integration, AT&T invited Evslin "to come and develop their internet strategy." Back then, Evslin says, AT&T didn't really have a clear plan for the internet. The company had tinkered with proprietary networks, but Evslin reckoned AT&T should become an ISP. "AT&T always had illusions about being a content provider," he says. Evslin also favored all-you-can-eat pricing, which smaller providers had attempted but AT&T had yet to try. "There was a lot of debate internally, people saying 'you can't launch a new service in less than seven years.'" Considering how quickly things were moving - and still are - seven years was a lifetime. "I said, 'the solution to that is launch it fast and then adapt.'" WorldNet offered straightforward internet access to customers accustomed to portals, proprietary networks, and some heart-stopping telephone bills. Demand grew so quickly that AT&T had to control sign-ups lest the service earn the "America On Hold" nickname occasionally and unkindly applied to America Online. With the internet in the ascendant, Evslin became interested in another technology: voice over IP. This, he acknowledges, "was an impossible sale inside AT&T." And so, in 1997, Evslin moved on again to found ITXC, a wholesale VoIP carrier. ®

title: AI is helping states clear decades of legislative clutter
teaser: Stanford HAI used AI to scan 500 million words of state law, finding "policy sludge" hindering government productivity across all 50 states.
summary:
Stanford HAI researchers are pioneering the use of AI to tackle governmental inefficiencies caused by 'policy sludge.' By scanning 500 million words of state law across all 50 states, they have mapped out outdated provisions and obsolete requirements that slow down government productivity. This technology is showing how AI can reshape legal practice, but it highlights a critical need for institutions to adapt.

Beyond legal aid, the discussion emphasizes human-centered approaches: Emma Brunskill developed a statistical test to determine when personalized interventions (in medicine or training) are truly beneficial. Overall, the article underscores that while AI development is rapid, efforts must focus on ensuring technological progress genuinely enhances, rather than diminishes, human dignity and capabilities.
author: Stanford HAI
content: Policymakers, academics, healthcare providers, AI developers, and patient advocates convened by Stanford HAI identify critical gaps in how we regulate AI tools used for therapy and emotional support. Outdated provisions, obsolete reporting requirements, and bureaucratic "policy sludge" slow government productivity and cost millions in staff time. Stanford HAI and RegLab researchers scanned 500 million words of state law across all 50 states to map the problem, and are now giving governments the tool to clear the clutter. AI is reshaping legal practice faster than the profession can evaluate it. Fixing legal AI's transparency problem will require more than just better metrics-it will require rethinking the institutions responsible for building them. HUMAN-CENTERED PERSPECTIVES How should we think about the field of law and AI? Stanford HAI Senior Fellows Daniel Ho , Julian Nyarko , and Christopher Manning and HAI Managing Director Vanessa Parli convened a group of lawyers, computer scientists, and social scientists for a special feature in the scientific journal PNAS to explore the appropriate role of AI in law and the role that law has in helping to govern this technology. A new white paper from the Stanford Accelerator for Learning, in collaboration with ETS, examines what responsible assessment looks like in the AI era. It includes insights from HAI Associate Director Emma Brunskill and HAI Faculty Affiliate Victor Lee . When does personalizing interventions in medicine, education, or job training produce real-world benefits? HAI Associate Director Emma Brunskill and Stanford postdoc Zhaoqi Li built a statistical test to measure when personalization is actually worth it. Too often, AI is built without understanding the people it affects. This fall, Stanford HAI and Stanford d.school will bring social sector leaders to campus for a hands-on program that integrates human-centered design with AI development. Join the fall cohort → This two-day workshop hosted at the University of Chicago brings together data science graduate students and postdocs at a critical point in their academic careers. Applications close August 3 at 11:59pm CT. Apply today → AI is changing not just what researchers can study, but how they study it. This conference, hosted by the Stanford Causal Science Center and the Graduate School of Business, brings together leading academics and practitioners to explore the frontier of data-driven research-from AI-assisted workflows and causal inference to the evolving relationship between human expertise and machine intelligence. Learn more → The defining challenge of our era is ensuring technological progress doesn't come at the expense of human dignity. This daylong conference takes up that challenge directly: examining the research, policies, and design methods required to put AI tools in human hands that augment, rather than replace, our creativity and independence. title: HP’s HyperX Omen 15 isn’t quite the budget-friendly gaming laptop its predecessor was
teaser: At $1,200, the Omen 15 delivers RTX 5050 gaming performance, but buyers must weigh the premium price against its budget-friendly predecessor.
summary: The HP HyperX Omen 15 is reviewed as an entry-level gaming laptop that sacrifices affordability for modern features. While it offers a brighter 16:10 display and the RTX 5050 GPU, its $1,200 starting price—up from $800 for the Victus 15—makes it far from budget-friendly. Key specs include an Intel Core 5 210H chip, 16GB DDR5 RAM, and a 512GB SSD. Performance is rated serviceable for modern games at 1080p/1200p (Medium settings with DLSS), though it struggles with battery life and storage capacity. The laptop’s strengths are its display and future upgrade potential, but its limited port selection and high cost diminish its overall appeal.
author: Antonio G. Di Benedetto
content: The HP HyperX Omen 15, which I first saw at CES , replaces the HP Victus 15 , a longtime bestselling budget gaming laptop. The Victus cost just $800, or less when on sale, and was a good entry point to decent laptop gaming. The Omen 15 has nice little upgrades over the Victus. Its RTX 5050 Laptop GPU can play 2026's latest games, albeit on low-ish settings. But it's also got a brighter 16:10 aspect ratio display with higher refresh rate, and a 1080p webcam to make it a little better for non-gaming stuff. I'd call it a working-class gaming laptop, but thanks to RAMageddon , the Omen 15 starts at $1,200 - a far cry from the $800 that made its predecessor so appealing. But laptop prices are way up across the board, and if you want current-gen gaming hardware, this is about as cheap as you're going to find it. $1199 The Good Affordable-ish gaming performance in a decent to solid package Fine for 1080p / 1200p gaming and light content creation 165Hz refresh rate on a fairly bright screen Upgradeable DDR5 RAM and NVMe SSD (with two slots for each) The Bad Not as affordable the HP Victus 15 it replaces Only one of the USB ports is USB-C - and not even Thunderbolt No face or fingerprint unlocking Keyboard, trackpad, and speakers range from okay to bad Screen: C Webcam: C Keyboard: C Trackpad: D Port selection: C Speakers: C Number of ugly stickers to remove: 3 Our HyperX Omen 15 review unit is a $1,199 configuration sold through Walmart with an eight-core Intel Core 5 210H "Raptor Lake" chip, RTX 5050 discreet GPU, 16GB of DDR5 RAM, and 512GB SSD. There are pricier Omen 15 configs out there with RTX 5070 GPUs and OLED screens, but that's like spending Acura money on a Honda Civic. On the lower end, HP still has a Victus 15 config with the RTX 5050 for $900, but it has 8GB of RAM - that's not really tenable, especially for playing the latest games. The good news is that the Omen 15 with an RTX 5050 is pretty serviceable for playing games at its 1920 x 1200 native resolution. Last-gen games like Control can get a smooth 70 to 80fps on High preset while using DLSS. Cyberpunk 2077 can run on the Ultra preset (no ray tracing) with DLSS set to Quality and get 60 to 70fps- sometimes dipping down to 40 while driving with lots of stuff onscreen. Standard frame generation boosts it to 95 to 105fps, and 70s to low 80s in a car. Multi Frame Gen, which you don't get on last-gen GPUs, can push that ever further if you don't mind more "fake frames." Newer games are a more Medium to Low affair. For example, Helldivers 2 runs comfortably at just above 60fps on its Medium preset with DLSS set to Quality - though it dips into the 40s when the bug guts hit the fan. But Battlefield 6 was lower, down in the 50fps range while running Medium preset with DLSS cranked to Performance. I also tested Halo: Campaign Evolved , which defaulted to its Very Low preset, where it looked like a potato. On Low settings, with DLSS set to Medium, it mustered between 50 to 60fps, but with frequent drops into the 40s with lots of enemies onscreen. On the right, an ethernet jack and one USB-A. On the left, a 3.5mm audio jack, one USB-A, and the power connector. On the rear, HDMI 2.1 and one USB-C. Seriously, where's the rest? While playing all these games, the fans kicked up to a decent volume, but they weren't obnoxiously loud, and the chassis stayed reasonably cool. The hottest point, a small spot under the chassis, rose to 113 degrees Fahrenheit / 45 Celsius. But the main areas that normally make contact with your hands or lap didn't get too warm - pretty good thermals for a somewhat compact gaming laptop. So the RTX 5050 GPU and its 8GB of VRAM can get by with the latest graphically intense games, so long as you're not expecting a visual powerhouse. But what about living with the rest of the laptop? Much of the Omen 15's price has gone to its specs. That means there are some rough edges showing in the usual areas. The trackpad has a responsive mechanical click, but if you pick up the laptop by either of its front corners the chassis flexes and causes an accidental click. This is common in mostly plastic laptops, but still annoying. The keyboard has decent enough tactility when typing. But even though I know gamers love a number pad, it makes this 15-inch laptop feel cramped. I don't enjoy typing on it like I have other HP laptops. The speakers? A little muddy-sounding - especially for music. And the ports? It has HDMI 2.1 and gigabit ethernet, which is great, but only one USB-C to go with its two USB-A ports. And all of them are a modest 10Gbps - not particularly speedy compared to USB4 or Thunderbolt 4. Gaming laptops are supposed to have ports aplenty, but this is just ports apassable. 1/7 The screen does a decent job controlling glare. Aside from its gaming performance, the Omen 15's other strength is its screen. The 1920 x 1200 IPS panel isn't particularly special, but at 400 nits it's decently bright and it has nice contrast and colors. It's good for games, and fine for productivity work and light content creation. I did a bit of Lightroom Classic editing on the Omen 15, and my 50-megapixel RAW files were workable at a modest clip. (It helped that I was editing a batch of under 50 images, and not, like, 2,000.) The bigger problem with trying to do creative things was the Omen's paltry 512GB of storage. It fills up quickly when games like Battlefield 6 take up 142GB. There's a second M.2 slot for another drive, just as there's a second RAM slot, which is great for future upgrades - but boy will that cost you right now . You can hold out for RAM and SSD prices to come back down to Earth, but if that takes as long as it's expected to, the Omen 15 might feel pretty outdated by then. The Omen was also fine for my everyday work: Chrome tabs, four virtual desktops, Signal, Slack, music streaming, etc. While the 1080p webcam is a little grainy and slightly low in saturation, it looks fine on video calls. The main barrier to getting work done on the Omen 15 is that its battery never lasted me more than five and a half hours. That's far from the worst for gaming laptops, but keep that chunky power adapter with its barrel plug nearby. That HyperX lid logo still doesn't look great to me, but I'm getting used to ignoring it. The HyperX Omen 15 is a decent gaming laptop. It's just not the value the Victus 15 used to be. But neither is anything else. Absent a really good sale, you're going to pay over $1,000 for anything with the RTX 5050, and usually a lot more. But buying into even the bottom rung of the 50-series gets you all of Nvidia's latest features, like Multi Frame Gen and whatever DLSS 5 eventually shapes up to be. Last-gen 40-series or AMD GPUs aren't bad options, but Multi Frame Gen can help keep frame rates playable for longer. It's still worth looking for those sales, though. HP, Best Buy, and Walmart often have deals on most of HP's product line. Even now, there's an Omen 16 with an RTX 5060 GPU and slightly larger (but dimmer) screen for just $100 more than the Omen 15. RAMageddon makes buying a new gaming laptop daunting. If you need to buy now and you don't want to go open-box or secondhand, you just have to come to terms with the fact that you're going to be paying higher prices than equivalent models from a year or two ago - even in the "entry level." Considering the circumstances, the Omen 15 is an okay value at $1,200 for getting into laptop gaming. HyperX Omen 15 specs (as reviewed) Display: 15.3-inch 1920 x 1200 165Hz IPS, 400 nits, anti-glare CPU: Intel Core 5 210H (Raptor Lake, 8 cores) GPU: Nvidia GeForce RTX 5050 RAM: 16GB DDR5 (two SODIMM slots, user-accessible) Storage: 512GB NVMe M.2 (two slots, user-accessible) Webcam: 1080p Connectivity: Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.3 Ports: 2x USB-A 10Gbps, 1x USB-C 10Gbps, AC power (barrel plug), HDMI 2.1, RJ-45 gigabit ethernet, 3.5mm combo audio jack Biometrics: none (lockscreen password only) Weight: 5 pounds / 2.27kg Dimensions: 13.5 x 9.96 x 0.89 - 0.93 inches / 342.9 x 252.98 x 22.61 - 23.62mm Battery: 70Wh Price: $1,199 Photography by Antonio G. title: 🚨 Cheap intelligence and 100 invites for Poke AI
teaser: The chat-like AI assistant Poke has been acquired by coding startup Cognition, aiming to inject 'personality' into their flagship agent, Devin.
summary:
Poke, the highly engaging AI messaging assistant from The Interaction Company of California, was acquired by Cognition for a deal valuing the company at a 'low nine figures.' This acquisition is significant because it merges Poke’s distinctive, friendly chat model with Cognition's powerful coding agent, Devin. Instead of operating like cold tools, Poke interacts familiarly, using humor and slang, making users feel they have a helpful 'colleague,' which Cognition aims to replicate in Devin.

The strategic move highlights that the *user experience* (the interaction layer) is becoming as valuable as raw AI model power. Poke has achieved massive adoption, exchanging over 100 million messages in three months and getting approved for Apple's Messages for Business platform. Long-term plans include integrating Poke with Cognition’s advanced SWE-1.7 model to enhance reliability and enable Poke to orchestrate multiple coding tasks within Devin.
author: TestingCatalog AI News
content: Greetings! Compared to the rest of July, this week was relatively quiet. The biggest story was the continued decline in AI costs. Both OpenAI and DeepSeek announced updates in this area, significantly lowering prices and putting pressure on many other cost-efficient models. This should have been especially noticeable for Google. Since there is still no competitive Pro model, Gemini 3.6 Flash also came under pressure. At the same time, we won't be getting AI Studio for mobile, although Google did ship a few new features for the desktop experience. Meanwhile, Seedance 2.5 was finally released, and Kimi K3 became open source! As a result, many AI providers can now host and serve the model on their own infrastructure. There is also good news for builders! Pokee is inviting you to get early access to their upcoming updates and features before the broader release. You'll get credits to build with, and optional rewards for publishing what you make. Pokee AI also offered our readers exclusive free month of Pokee Lite for the first 100 applicants . If you apply through the Google Form , you'll be among the first to test their new tools and start building on top of them. And now, let's break everything down! title: Xbox prices are increasing by up to €200 or £170
teaser: Xbox console prices are soaring! The 1TB Xbox Series X Disc model jumps to nearly €800/£670, marking a massive price increase for gamers.
summary: Xbox consoles are undergoing substantial price hikes across various models. The increases affect both the Series S and Series X, impacting players' budgets for next-gen gaming hardware. Specifically, the 512GB Xbox Series S is jumping to €499.99 / £429.99 (up from €349.99 / £299.99). Similarly, the 1TB Xbox Series X Digital will cost €749.99 / £619.99 (an increase from €549.99 / £449.99), and the 1TB Xbox Series X Disc version is now priced at €799.99 / £669.99, up from its previous cost of €599.99 / £499.99.
author: Terrence O’Brien

title: Show HN: Sprocket – The Best AI Agent for Hardware and Software Development
teaser: Sprocket is an AI development agent that doesn't just code—it can buy hardware parts and SaaS subscriptions autonomously.
summary: Sprocket is a comprehensive AI agent aimed at streamlining hardware and software development. Its capabilities are broad, including creating schematics in React, generating detailed Bills of Material (BOMs), writing code, and leveraging web context for maximum reliability. Uniquely, Sprocket can autonomously purchase physical components or SaaS subscriptions from any site when instructed. Users can run the agent via a command line interface (CLI) with options like `sprocket --web`. Development requires specific environments, such as Bun 1.x/Node.js 24.x+ or a stable Rust toolchain.
author: amronos
content:
Goal : To make the world's best platform for developing hardware and software. Sprocket is a lightweight agent that can create hardware designs and write code. Sprocket retrieves best-in-class context from the web for everything it does. It is therefore incredibly reliable.
In terms of hardware design, Sprocket can make beautiful schematics in React, create your BOM, and create detailed assembly instructions. And here's the best part : Sprocket can (on its own) buy anything from any website when you tell it to do so. From hardware parts to SaaS subscriptions. Sprocket Demo Note You can run Sprocket using any of the ways defined below with no impact on Sprocket's capabilities or performance.
The desktop app may take more RAM than using Sprocket through your browser. The above runs Sprocket through your browser unless you have the desktop app installed. Install it for your OS from the latest GitHub Release Artifacts and run it. npm i -g @spikonado/sprocket
sprocket The above runs Sprocket through your browser unless you have the desktop app installed. To always open a tab in your browser when using Sprocket, use the --web flag: Pass a directory to open or reconnect that workspace in a new thread: sprocket . sprocket --web ../my-robot Sprocket remembers attached workspaces and local server sessions between launches.
Local state lives in $HOME/.sprocket (or %USERPROFILE%\.sprocket on Windows when HOME is unset).
Override with SPROCKET_DATA_DIR . Command Behavior sprocket serve Run the local server in the foreground without launching a client. sprocket serve --api-only Serve only /api ; intended for development (see Development ). Run sprocket --help or sprocket serve --help for all options. Common Sprocket server overrides are available as environment variables: Variable Purpose SPROCKET_DATA_DIR Directory for pairing, sessions, and workspace state. SPROCKET_PORT Local server port; defaults to 17731 for installed use. SPROCKET_HOST Bind host; defaults to 127.0.0.1 . SPROCKET_DESKTOP_EXECUTABLE Full path to the desktop executable to be used by the Sprocket CLI. PUBLIC_CONVEX_URL Convex deployment used by the agent runtime. SPROCKET_STATIC_DIR Web build to serve instead of the bundled build. Bun 1.x, version 1.3.9 or newer Node.js 24.x, version 24.14 or newer A current stable Rust toolchain Install dependencies: Start the browser development environment: After creating a convex deployment and configuring authkit following the instructions, configure the Convex deployment with the API key for each model provider you want to enable. This runs Vite at http://localhost:5173 and the Rust API at http://127.0.0.1:7731 , with development state kept in .sprocket-dev inside the repository.
To develop against Electron instead, run: cargo test bun run test bun run build
prek run -a Create a local Electron installer package with: Artifacts are written to apps/desktop/dist/ as sprocket-desktop-* ( .AppImage / .dmg / .exe depending on the host OS).
Published installers come from GitHub Releases; the sprocket CLI is published separately on npm. If 17731 is already occupied, set SPROCKET_PORT before launching. If sprocket opens the browser instead of the desktop app, install sprocket-desktop from GitHub Releases onto PATH , or set SPROCKET_DESKTOP_EXECUTABLE . Unsigned macOS and Windows desktop builds may need a Gatekeeper / SmartScreen override the first time you open them. Contact aarav@spikonado.com for help.

title: Eric Trump-backed Space-Eyes to go public via $638M SPAC merger
teaser: Eric Trump's backed Space-Eyes is heading public via $638M SPAC merger, betting big on AI counter-drone technology.
summary: Defense tech startup Space-Eyes plans a major IPO via a SPAC merger with McKinley Acquisition Corp., valuing the combined business at $638 million. Specialized in AI technologies for countering drone warfare and providing geospatial intelligence, Space-Eyes currently operates on annual revenues of about $1 million but is negotiating contracts worth $35 million over five years. The company’s core offerings include SeaWatch, a maritime tracking platform, and Morpheus, an AI counter-drone system. Eric Trump, already a major investor, will serve as a strategic adviser following the transaction. SPACs are shell companies used to take private firms public without a traditional IPO, though such methods have seen mixed success recently.
author: Mike Wheatley
content: Space-Eyes , a defense technology startup backed by U.S President Donald Trump's son Eric Trump, has revealed it's planning to go public through a merger with a special purpose acquisition company called McKinley Acquisition Corp. The deal will value the combined businesses at around $638 million, Reuters reported . Eric Trump recently became the third-largest private investor in Space-Eyes, which has so far operated primarily as a research and development company and generates around $1 million in annual revenue, four people familiar with the business told Reuters. Following the completion of the transaction , he will serve as a strategic adviser to the combined business, having already introduced a number of prospective board candidates to the company's management. Miami-based Space-Eyes is a developer of artificial intelligence technologies focused on countering drone warfare and geospatial intelligence systems that are marketed to governments and militaries. Following the acquisition, the company reportedly intends to scale up its business by using third-party manufacturers. This will allow it to compete for government contracts in multiple countries and also target corporate clients ranging from data center operators to cruise companies, Reuters' sources said. Space-Eyes, led by founder and Chief Executive Officer Jatin Bains and Chief Operating Officer Dylan Monroe, describes itself as a software company that combines data from satellites, radio-frequency sensors, radar and other sources. It says it uses that information to detect, track and respond to drone-related threats and provide geospatial intelligence in real-time. Its main products include SeaWatch , which is a maritime intelligence platform that's able to track vessels using satellite and sensor data, and Morpheus , an AI-powered counter-drone platform that's focused on mitigating autonomous aerial threats. The report added that Space-Eyes is currently negotiating contracts worth around $35 million over a five-year period. Its existing contracts reportedly bring in around $300,000 to $400,000 annually, the sources added. The contracts pertain to its software being deployed to monitor drug trafficking in the Caribbean, power defense applications in the Middle East and prevent contraband being smuggled into U.S. prisons via drones. In his role as a strategic adviser, Eric Trump will help to advise the company on the latest security threats posed by drones and similar emerging technologies, drawing on his experience with security issues affecting the White House. "He is an important adviser that connects us to people and opportunities, and he is an adviser that brings intelligence," one of the sources told Reuters. The transaction will generate around $251.7 million in gross proceeds, including funds held in McKinley's trust account and a planned private investment in public equity financing, the report said. Space-Eyes is betting on the growing interest among investors in defense technology firms that use AI to combat drones, power autonomous systems and provide battlefield intelligence. Reuters reports that the company was inspired by the software and data analytics firm Palantir Technologies Inc., which is a major U.S. government contractor and reported an adjusted operating margin of more than 60% in its most recent earnings call. That compares with the single-digit margins of traditional defense companies. SPACs are shell companies that raise cash through an initial public offering then use that money to merge with private firms and take them public. They became popular as an alternative to holding an IPO from 2020 to 2022, but many companies that went public through that route struggled to achieve their growth targets. Reuters said the deal taking Space-Eyes public is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to shareholder and regulatory approval. The company will then start trading on the Nasdaq index under the ticker symbol "CUAS," which is a reference to the term "counter-unmanned aerial systems." title: Slopulism is taking over America
teaser: Economists warn that laws forcing self-checkout discounts will fail, paradoxically leading grocery stores to fire human cashiers instead of protecting them.
summary: The article analyzes proposed policies—like requiring discounts for using self-checkouts—arguing that such initiatives fail their stated goals through economic principles. The author demonstrates that, due to intense market competition in the highly competitive grocery sector, a discount on automated checkout would actually force stores to raise prices across the board rather than simply lowering them. This overcharging strategy would be undercut by competitors offering cheaper alternatives, leading stores to ultimately fire human cashiers and replace them with more self-checkout machines. The author labels such policy attempts 'slopulism,' defining it as a dangerous form of populism that promotes policies despite lacking economic viability.
author: Noahpinion
content: Would you like to see an example of a badly conceived policy? Here you go: The bill to require discounts for self-checkout will probably not pass. But what's notable is that if this bill did pass, it would have exactly the opposite of the effect its creators want. The stated justification is that customers are doing unpaid labor by scanning and bagging their own groceries, and that this discount would compensate them for that effort. But the bill is part of a more general effort to disincentivize automation in the retail industry, in order to protect working-class jobs: Rhode Island was the first state in the U.S. to enact statewide self-checkout restrictions with its Restrictions on Self-Service Checkout Stations Act , which takes effect January 1, 2027. The act requires grocery stores to have at least one human-operated checkout station for every three self-service stations during peak hours...Similar legislation has either been introduced, enacted or considered in additional states including California, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Washington, and Ohio. The standard objection to this bill, I suppose, would be that self-checkout already gives shoppers a discount, because it allows stores to save money on hiring human labor, and that these savings get passed on to consumers in the form of lower prices. That argument is correct as far as it goes, but it means the debate ends up as one of technocracy versus populism - protecting the livelihoods of a few cashiers versus giving a huge number of consumers very slightly lower prices. There's no simple or easy conclusion to that debate. But in the case of New York's proposed self-checkout discount, the problem is that the bill would actually make grocery stores fire human cashiers in favor of more self-checkout . To understand why this is true, first imagine an incredibly extreme version of the policy. Imagine that instead of 10%, you made a law forcing grocery stores to give a 90% discount for self-checkout. This is exactly the same as forcing stores to charge 10x for using a human cashier. Who would pay 10x for groceries, just to use a human cashier? Basically no one. So everyone would go use the self-checkout machines, and stores would have no need for human cashiers at all. But wait, you may be thinking. How could any store afford to give a 90% discount on groceries? The same way they give discounts for seniors and students at movie theaters. You just raise the sticker price, so that the price people actually pay after the discount is the same as before. So instead of keeping human-cashier prices the same and cutting prices for self-checkout, what stores would actually do if you made them give 10% discounts for self-checkout is to raise prices across the board - not by 10%, but by enough so that overall revenue is just about the same as it was before. How do we know this is what will happen? Because the grocery store industry is very competitive. Profit margins are almost always between 1.5% and 2.8%, which is very low compared to the average industry : It's not just profit margins that demonstrate this - there are tons of grocery stores, and new ones enter the market all the time . This means that if grocery stores tried to respond to the New York bill by getting rid of self-checkout and using only human cashiers - in order to charge higher prices and make higher profits - other stores would undercut them by offering self-checkout with big discounts. People would flock to those other stores, and the stores that tried to overcharge would lose business until they, too, put in the self-checkout machines. This is kind of like if you told grocery stores to charge 10% more for Skippy peanut butter than for Jif peanut butter. Obviously stores would want to stock more Skippy, because they'd earn more money on each sale. But obviously consumers would want to buy more Jif, because it was cheaper. At the end of the day, the consumers would win, because consumers tend to win out when an industry is highly competitive . Some people would still buy Skippy, because some people just really like Skippy more, but overall, forcing one brand of peanut butter to cost more than another brand means you'll have less of it on the shelves. By the exact same reasoning, forcing stores to charge more for purchases scanned by human cashiers will end up getting a lot of cashiers fired and replaced with self-checkout machines. As policies go, this example isn't particularly hard to explain, or to understand. If you ask any economist, or any good AI, they'll give basically the same answer, in different words. It would be a good question on an undergrad microeconomics exam. But when I tried to explain this on X , some people had a lot of trouble understanding: The idea of a 10% discount on self-checkout as a way to incentivize human employment is pure "slopulism" - stuff that seems like populism, but wouldn't achieve the results that people want from the policy. It's snake oil that sells well based on people's inability to see the consequences of what they're being sold. Slopulism is an inevitable outgrowth of populism. Once people decide that technocrats, elites, experts, and gatekeepers aren't worth listening to, they become vulnerable to all sorts of policy scams. In general, these scams fall into two categories: Accidental scams, where the people making the policy just don't understand what they're doing Ideological scams, where ideologues sell the public on an ideologically-driven policy by pretending it offers benefits that it doesn't really offer The second of these is more dangerous than the first. Slopulism that arises out of pure ignorance is very hard to correct, and social media - which elevates the dumbest and loudest at the expense of the most well-informed - probably makes it harder. But in the end, patience, education, and reason can overcome accidental slopulism - and AI may help a lot . But when slopulist ideas are being promoted by smart people with ulterior motives, it can be a lot harder to wake the populace up. At that point, there's the danger that slopulism becomes a bipartisan equilibrium , with each party's ideologues executing a coup against the reasonable moderates by appealing to slopulist instincts.

title: Malaysia is reportedly shutting down Balaji Srinivasan’s Network School
teaser: Balaji Srinivasan's Network School faces shutdown in Malaysia amid accusations of poor living conditions, but plans continue for a new base in Kazakhstan.
summary: The Network School, a community promoting techno-optimism led by Balaji Srinivasan, has been ordered shut down by the Malaysian government. Billing itself as a step toward building a new society—a goal detailed in his book 'The Network State'—the school was located in an abandoned hotel and served as both a tech incubator and retreat. While attendees complained about poor conditions like moldy rooms, the program’s closure is reportedly due to licensing issues. Following the news from The Wall Street Journal, Srinivasan confirmed he renounced American citizenship (now declared Singaporean) and announced that a new campus agreement has been made for Kazakhstan.
author: Anthony Ha
content: The Malaysian government has ordered the shutdown of a startup-centric community called the Network School, according to The Wall Street Journal . Billing itself as "a frontier community for techno-optimists," the Network School reportedly grew out of entrepreneur and investor Balaji Srinivasan's conviction that the United States is in irreversible decline; Srinivasan has said his goal is "to start a new country." So the Network School is supposed to represent the first step in a seven-stage plan (outlined in Srinivasan's book "The Network State" ) for building a new society. Based in an abandoned Malaysian hotel, the WSJ described the program as "part tech incubator, part self-improvement retreat." Attendees, however, complained about moldy rooms, as well as a dearth of women and nightlife. After receiving questions from the WSJ, Srinivasan - who apparently renounced his American citizenship in 2023 - published a lengthy post on X declaring himself "a proud Singaporean" and complaining that the WSJ was working on a "hit piece" that would make him look like "an odd duck [...] as opposed to an early adopter." And although the current Malaysian campus will reportedly need to shut down due to licensing issues, Srinivasan recently announced a new agreement for a campus in Kazakhstan.

title: Fender’s CEO seems to think your bandmates are just analog AI
teaser: Fender's CEO claims AI music assistance is nothing new; he calls 'cover music' an analog form of AI.
summary: According to Fender's CEO, AI assistance in music is not a novel concept. He argues that certain processes, like performing 'cover music,' have functioned as an analog form of AI for decades. The technology’s true potential, he suggests, lies in its ability to support original songwriting and collaboration. Instead of limiting creativity to repeating existing songs (covers), modern AI tools can act much like collaborative bandmates—helping people move beyond old material toward developing unique compositions.
author: Terrence O’Brien
content: Cole's philosophy is that AI in music is nothing new. "I think AI has existed in music as long as there's been recorded music," he says. While the biggest barrier to playing guitar is the time it takes to learn the instrument, it's the second barrier, writing songs, where he believes AI plays a part. "I actually believe cover music has been sort of analog AI for a long time," says Cole. Those that don't yet have the skills to write their own songs can play the songs written by their favourite artists instead. "I listened a lot to REM, U2, The Smiths and The Cure, and at some point I got sick of just listening to them. I wanted to play it, so I learned to play guitar." Those taking their first steps into writing, according to Cole, can also lean on a second analogue form of AI: their band mates. You might just have a chorus or a riff to start with but then the drummer or bassist can add to it, and a song is born. AI can also play this role. "I actually think that we are in the brink of freeing up people to move beyond the same old covers and to really get into working like they do with their bands," says Cole.

To entice subscribers back, the newsletter offers access to its 'top prompt library,' which includes key prompts used for daily AI work. Readers are prompted to complete a three-question quiz covering their reasons for learning about AI, preferred content types, and what they miss most about The Neuron. This serves as an incentive to stay subscribed and keep one's AI knowledge current.
author: The Neuron
content: We ran a sophisticated AI analysis (okay, fine, we just noticed)-and you haven't opened The Neuron in a while. Did you get stuck in a ChatGPT rabbit hole? Get replaced by a chatbot? title: Skylight’s smart calendars are up to $90 off during its back-to-school sale
teaser: Manage family chaos during back-to-school! Skylight's smart calendars are up to $90 off through August 9th, helping you keep every schedule synced.
summary: Parents dealing with busy schedules can benefit from Skylight's smart calendars, which are on sale through August 9th. The sales offer discounts up to $90 on models ranging from 10-inch to the largest wall-mounted 27-inch Calendar Max. Functionally, the system allows every household member a color-coded profile and syncs events from major platforms like Google and Apple. Key features include using AI to convert various digital sources (photos, emails) into calendar entries, and facilitating shared task management. Furthermore, users can create shared lists for chores or groceries and integrate with services like Instacart.
author: Sheena Vasani
content: The start of a new school year can feel hectic, as parents juggle their kids' classes, extracurriculars and sports on top of work, appointments, and other responsibilities. It's easy for things to slip through the cracks, but Skylight's shared smart calendars can help keep everyone on track, and from August 2nd through August 9th they're up to $90 off. The sale includes the 10-inch Skylight Calendar for $119.99 ($50 off) , the 15-inch Skylight Calendar 2 for $259.99 ($20 off) , and the 27-inch Skylight Calendar Max for $479.99 ($90 off) . The 10-inch model takes up the least amount of space, though the newer, larger 15-inch Calendar 2 features faster performance, a brighter display, and swappable magnetic frames. The 27-inch Calendar Max, meanwhile, offers the sharpest and largest screen and must be mounted to the wall (the other models can stand on a table or be mounted), making it the easiest option for large families to view from across the room. Regardless of which model you choose, every Skylight Calendar includes the same set of organizational features. Each member of your household can have their own color-coded profile, and each can sync events from Google, Outlook, Apple, Cozi, or Yahoo calendars. You can also create shared lists for groceries, chores, and other to-dos that everyone can access from the calendar or the companion mobile app, and even send your grocery list to Instacart with a couple of taps. Built-in weather forecasts also can help you plan around upcoming events, and you can also share calendar access with family members and trusted contacts. You get even more perks if you subscribe to the $79 per year Plus Plan (the first month of the service is free to try). Skylight uses AI to automatically turn emails, photos, flyers, and spreadsheets into calendar entries. It also adds meal planning, tools for assigning and rewarding completed chores, and a mode that displays your photos like a digital picture frame.

title: Rachika Nayar’s Heaven Come Crashing is an instrumental epic of desperate longing
teaser: Rachika Nayar’s 'Heaven Come Crashing' delivers an instrumental epic of desperate longing, building from drone to a sudden, massive drum and bass beat drop.
summary: Rachika Nayar’s album, 'Heaven Come Crashing,' is a deeply emotional instrumental journey that utilizes lush, guitar-heavy ambient music rather than traditional vocals or percussion to capture desperate longing. The record features contributions from Maria BC's ethereal vocals on tracks like the title song and the powerful closer, "Our Wretched Fate." While many tracks are largely drum-free, they build toward explosive moments, exemplified by the massive beat drop in the title track. Notably, a piece originally titled "Death and Love" is called "Death and Limerence," focusing instead on unhealthy romantic obsession. The album explores themes of emotional recklessness through heavily processed guitars and atmospheric soundscapes.
author: Terrence O’Brien
content: Two minutes and thirty seconds into the title track of Rachika Nayar's Heaven Come Crashing , an absolutely massive drum and bass beat drops. As a fan of Nayar's debut record Our Hands Against The Dusk , it caught me off guard. That album has no percussion on it at all. Heaven Comes Crashing is almost entirely drum-free, too. There are some rapid-fire mechanical hi-hats on the second track, "Tetramorph," and the back half of track six, "Gayatri," has what sounds like a snare buried deep in the mix. But it isn't until track seven that Nayar delivers an unexpected drum explosion, before immediately retreating to the soothing wash of "Sleepless," just one song later. Nayar's unique brand of guitar-heavy ambient-adjacent music plays almost like a version of M83 from an alternate universe. One where instead of turning to '80s pop music for inspiration, Anthony Gonzalez mined his instrumental epics for every last drop of emotion. Heaven Comes Crashing is as emotionally heavy as the title would imply but uses surprisingly few words to get there. The only vocals come courtesy of Maria BC, who floats over the title track and the stunning album closer "Our Wretched Fate," where she worldlessly belts out her laments. There are lyrics on "Heaven Comes Crashing," but they're almost indecipherable as Maria BC whispers beneath an ocean of flailing guitar lines and sparkling drones: Is it morning? I don't remember going to sleep How can we face the day Like this? You throw down your arms and count to see How deep it is Instead of words, Nayar turns to heavily processed guitar, lonesome textures, and the occasional burst of trance chords to capture the desperate longing at the album's core. But the album is also an indictment of the sort of abandon that often accompanies unbridled passion. It's bookended by "Our Wretched Fantasy" and "Our Wretched Fate," betraying a certain disgust for its own emotional recklessness. Track three isn't "Death and Love"; it's "Death and Limerence" - opting to spotlight unhealthy romantic obsession rather than fulfilling emotional partnership, through U2-esque guitar lines that eventually drown beneath heavily reverbed and out-of-tune tremolo-picked notes. That's followed by the unease of "Nausea," which builds from an unsteady drone to maximalist panic of '90s synths and one of the simplest and prettiest guitar melodies on the record. The ambient emo of "Promises" follows, leading into "Gayatri," which ratchets up the energy and serves as a bridge to the explosive title track. Rachika Nayar's Heaven Comes Crashing is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Apple Music , Spotify , YouTube Music , Qobuz , and Deezer .
